claims.paper: Table 3.5-3 (chain pickerel, bioenergetics column); Table 4.3 (chain pickerel)
claims.claim: no chain pickerel set exists; the model uses the northern pike set of Bevelhimer et al. 1985

claims.quote: measured individual food consumption, conversion efficiency, growth, and metabolic rate for Ohio stocks

claims.location: p. 61 (PDF p. 6), Table 1; p. 60 (PDF p. 5), text after eq. 4
claims.conditions: ASSUMED, not fitted: b1 set equal to b2 = −0.18, which is Diana's (1982) respiration exponent for 5–1,200-g pike at 14 °C; the authors could not fit either exponent on their 9–53-g fish
claims.note: relevant to §5.8: the set's mass scaling was never fitted on the 9–53-g fish at all — it was borrowed from Diana's larger pike and assumed equal for consumption "convenient for this study"; only the intercepts and temperature terms were fitted

claims.claim: the set was fitted on 9–53-g pike eating minnows
claims.quote: Because we used a narrow range of sizes (9-53 g), values for b2
claims.conditions: 9.5–53.2 g is the respirometry sample (all three taxa pooled for one respiration curve); the consumption fish were 7.2–43.5 g initial (mean 19.3 g), fed live fathead minnows 25–40 % of their length
claims.note: the respiration curve was fitted to pike, muskellunge and tiger muskellunge together, not to pike alone

claims.claim: the set's respiration temperature slope is Q10 1.73
claims.quote: The m value of 0.055 corresponds to a Q10 of 1.73
claims.conditions: one exponential curve fitted to all three taxa at 5, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C, closed static respirometer, inactive fish ("low routine" metabolism)

claims.claim: 10 g is the floor of the fitted size range
claims.quote: Initial predator lengths were 125-210 mm; initial weights were 7.2-43.5 g
claims.conditions: consumption experiments 7.2–43.5 g initial; respirometry 9.5–53.2 g
claims.note: the floor is 7–10 g depending on the experiment; 10 g is a fair round number

claims.claim: Bevelhimer et al.'s consumption–temperature function is a cubic polynomial in the exponent with no hard upper cutoff
claims.quote: we decided that a third-order polynomial equation best
claims.conditions: ln Cmax = ln a1 + b1·ln B + xT + yT² + zT³; the authors warn against use outside 5–30 °C (p. 62)

claims.claim: consumption parameters of the FB4 northern pike set (Bevelhimer et al. 1985)
claims.conditions: northern pike (NP) row; Cmax in g g⁻¹ d⁻¹ wet mass

claims.claim: respiration parameters of the FB4 northern pike set
claims.quote: correction factor of 1.075. Although we did not include this correction factor
claims.conditions: one curve for all three taxa; the authors' model ran WITHOUT the ×1.075 log-retransformation bias correction
claims.note: 0.1025 × 24 / 1000 = 0.00246 g O₂ g⁻¹ d⁻¹; × 1.075 = 0.0026445, the code's RA. So FB4's RA includes the bias correction the authors describe but did not apply: 7.5 % above the published model. The value is defensible; cite it "as converted in FB4"

claims.paper: src/species.js:378 (RTO 0.1222 with RK1 1, RK4 0: activity multiplier)
claims.quote: the inclusion of the activity factor increases the metabolic rate by 13%
claims.conditions: activity durations and swimming speeds held constant across size, temperature and taxon

claims.claim: the set's waste and SDA terms
claims.quote: Specific dynamic action factor 0.14 … Egestion factor 0.20 … Excretion factor 0.07
claims.conditions: Brett & Groves (1979) averages for all fishes, no esocid data; S, f and u all as fractions of consumption C
claims.note: FB4 applies SDA and U to C − F: 0.14/0.8 = 0.175 and 0.07/0.8 = 0.0875 — the same budget. These losses are Brett & Groves's general values, not measured on esocids

claims.conditions: 860 cal/g wet, esocids and fathead minnows alike (R. Stein, unpublished data); no seasonal variation

claims.claim: the curve peaks at 24.6 °C because it was fit to small pike
claims.quote: These temperatures were 24.6, 26.7, and 23.5°C for northern pike, muskellunge, and tiger muskellunge
claims.conditions: optimum of the fitted Cmax polynomial; growth optimum in simulations 24 °C (p. 62), maximum observed growth at 25 °C (p. 67)
claims.note: the source attributes the warm optimum to a possibly warm-adapted Ohio stock, not to fish size

claims.claim: the set's consumption ceiling is 1.2–2.6× short below ~0.1–0.3 g
claims.note: a project comparison against larval data (Wieser et al. 1992 etc.), not a value of this source; the source only supplies the −0.18 exponent being extrapolated

notes: Every model value of the FB4 pike set matches Table 1 after FB4's conversions (RA includes the ×1.075 bias factor the authors mention but did not use; SDA and UA are re-based on C − F; RTO = ln 1.13; ED = 860 cal/g). Two framing points for the rewrite: (1) the set is not an adult set — it was built on hatchery young-of-year pike (and, for respiration, muskellunge and tiger muskellunge pooled) of 7–53 g; (2) neither mass exponent was fitted on these fish: b2 = −0.18 is Diana's (1982) value for 5–1,200-g pike and b1 was set equal to it. Bevelhimer's own losses (S 0.14, f 0.20, u 0.07) are Brett & Groves's all-fish averages. Model validation in the source: predicted growth fell within 1 SD of observed in 2-week trials except pike and muskellunge at 5 °C (p. 62).
